topics.title: A poem on observing closely: imagery and looking words

learn.hook: Hold a magnifying glass over an ordinary leaf, and suddenly it looks like a map of rivers! Close looking turns the ordinary into the amazing.
points: 'Magnifying Glass' is a poem about looking closely at small things and discovering wonder in them.
A magnifying glass is a convex lens (thicker in the middle) that makes things look bigger than they are.
Imagery means word pictures that appeal to the senses. Poets use imagery and metaphors to show what close looking reveals: 'a beetle's back becomes a shining shield'.

Looking words have different shades of meaning: observe and examine (look carefully), peer (look closely, as if it is hard to see), inspect (check for details or faults), glance and glimpse (look quickly or briefly).
Close observation is the first step of science and of good writing: notice details, colours, shapes, patterns and changes.

example.q: Read this original poem: 'Through my glass a beetle's back / Becomes a shining shield of black; / A leaf turns into a map of streams, / A drop of dew holds rainbow gleams.' Think it through: what does the leaf become, and why is that a good image?
steps: The poem says the leaf 'turns into a map of streams'.
Under a magnifying glass, the veins of a leaf look like rivers branching on a map.
This is a metaphor: it compares the leaf directly to a map.
It helps us see the leaf's tiny veins in a new way.
example.answer: The leaf becomes 'a map of streams', because its veins look like branching rivers when magnified.

learn.reallife: Scientists use magnifying lenses and microscopes, jewellers check gems with a small lens, and you can watch ants or study a flower's parts in your garden.

games.title: Looking words
pairs: look closely, as if it is hard to see
check carefully for details or faults
look steadily for a long time

games.title: About the magnifying poem
items: In the poem, the beetle's back becomes a shining shield.
That is the image in the first two lines.
A magnifying glass makes things look smaller.
A magnifying glass is a convex lens.
A convex lens is thicker in the middle and can magnify.
'A drop of dew holds rainbow gleams' describes colours seen in dew.
Light in the dewdrop shows rainbow colours.
To 'glimpse' something means to study it for a long time.
A glimpse is a quick, brief look.
Imagery means word pictures that appeal to the senses.
Imagery helps readers see, hear or feel what the poet describes.

quiz.q: Read: 'Through my glass a beetle's back / Becomes a shining shield of black.' What is the beetle's back compared to?
quiz.explain: The beetle's hard, shiny back is compared to a shining black shield.
quiz.mistake: Picks an image from another line

quiz.q: What kind of lens is a magnifying glass?
quiz.explain: A magnifying glass is a convex lens, thicker in the middle.

quiz.q: Read: 'A leaf turns into a map of streams.' This line is an example of ___.
quiz.explain: It compares a leaf directly to a map, without 'like' or 'as'.
quiz.mistake: Calls it a simile even though there is no 'like' or 'as'

quiz.q: Which word means 'to look at something carefully and in detail'?
quiz.explain: To examine is to look closely and carefully.
quiz.mistake: Picks a word for a quick look

quiz.q: Read: 'A drop of dew holds rainbow gleams.' What does the poet see in the dewdrop?
quiz.explain: 'Rainbow gleams' are flashes of rainbow colours in the dew.
quiz.mistake: Does not read the line closely

options: The pictures printed in the book
Word pictures that appeal to the senses
quiz.explain: Imagery is language that helps us see, hear, smell, taste or feel things in our mind.

quiz.q: Sita had to ___ at the tiny letters on the old coin to read them.
quiz.explain: To peer is to look very closely because something is hard to see.
quiz.mistake: Picks a word for a quick or careless look

quiz.q: What is the main message of a poem about a magnifying glass?
options: Looking closely reveals wonder in ordinary things
quiz.explain: The poem shows that careful looking makes small, everyday things amazing.
quiz.mistake: Focuses on one detail instead of the main idea

teach.ask: Gappu looked at a leaf through a magnifying glass and gasped! What did he discover, and why do poets love close looking?
teach.praise: Wow! The glass makes things bigger so I notice tiny details, and ordinary things turn amazing. Close looking is magic!
teach.nudge: What does the glass do to the leaf? What do you notice when you look closely?

topics.title: Curiosity: asking good questions and question tags

learn.hook: Why is the sky blue? How do ants find sugar? Every great discovery begins with a curious question!
points: Curiosity means a strong wish to know or learn. Curious (adjective) → curiosity (noun). Note the spelling: curiosity, not 'curiousity'.
Wh-questions ask for information: what, where, when, why, who, which, whose, how. 'Why do leaves change colour?'
Yes/no questions begin with a helping verb: Is, Are, Do, Does, Did, Can, Have. 'Does the lens make things bigger?'
In questions, the helping verb comes before the subject: 'Where does the beetle live?' (not 'Where the beetle lives?').

A question tag is a short question at the end of a sentence. A positive statement takes a negative tag and a negative statement takes a positive tag: 'It's a lens, isn't it?' 'You don't like spiders, do you?'

example.q: Think it through: Turn this observation into two good questions: 'The ants walk in a line towards the sugar.'
steps: A wh-question asking why: Why do the ants walk in a line?
A wh-question asking how: How do the ants find the sugar?
Check the order: helping verb 'do' comes before the subject 'the ants'.
example.answer: Why do the ants walk in a line? How do the ants find the sugar?

learn.reallife: Scientists, journalists and detectives all ask good questions. In class, asking 'Why?' and 'How?' helps you understand, not just remember.

items.text: The magnifying glass is useful, ___ it?
She can see the beetle, ___ she?
They went to the science fair, ___ they?
Ravi has finished his project, ___ he?

games.title: Build a question
games.prompt: Arrange the words to make a correct question

quiz.explain: The noun drops the 'u' from 'curious': curiosity.

quiz.q: Which question word asks for a reason?
quiz.explain: 'Why' asks for a reason: Why is the sky blue?

quiz.q: Which question is in the correct order?
quiz.explain: In a question, the helping verb 'does' comes before the subject 'the beetle'.
quiz.mistake: Uses statement word order in a question

quiz.q: Choose the correct question tag: 'It is raining, ___?'
quiz.explain: A positive statement with 'is' takes the negative tag 'isn't it?'
quiz.mistake: Uses a positive tag after a positive statement

quiz.q: Choose the correct question tag: 'You haven't seen my lens, ___?'
quiz.explain: A negative statement with 'haven't' takes the positive tag 'have you?'
quiz.mistake: Repeats the negative in the tag

quiz.explain: It begins with the helping verb 'Is' and can be answered with yes or no.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any question can be answered yes or no

quiz.q: Which word means 'eager to know or learn'?
quiz.explain: A curious person wants to know more.

quiz.q: Choose the correct question tag: 'Meena found a snail, ___?'
quiz.explain: 'Found' is simple past (positive), so the tag uses 'did' in the negative: didn't she?
quiz.mistake: Does not use 'did' for a simple past statement

teach.ask: Gappu is curious about everything but never knows how to ask! How do I make a good question in English?
teach.praise: Hooray! Start with a word like 'why' or 'how', put the helping verb before the subject, and end with a question mark. Why do worms wiggle?
teach.nudge: Which words can begin a question? Where does the helping verb go?
